source.excerpt: Management is the most noble of professions if it’s practiced well. No other occupation offers as many ways to help others learn and grow, take responsibility and be recognized for achievement, and contribute to the success of a team.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced Christensen page ↗ carries the full sentence in its 2010s section, cited to Christensen (2011) in Harvard Business Review, HBR’s 10 Must Reads on Managing Yourself (2011), p. 4.
That is a citation to a named work and a specific page, with no competing source anywhere in view — which is why this page is marked verified rather than attributed.

The limit, stated plainly: the publisher’s own text was not opened. hbr.org refused the connection from this run, and the Internet Archive’s scans of Christensen’s books are access-restricted. The wording and page here are adopted from the anchor source above, not independently re-derived from the printed page.
source.cutTag: HBR's 10 Must Reads on Managing Yourself (2011), p. 4
source.excerptNote: The quotation above is the form that circulates, and it stops at ‘learn and grow’. The documented sentence does not: it goes on to name two more things the job offers — responsibility that is recognised, and a share in a team’s success. The short version is faithful as far as it goes; it simply goes less far.

author.name: Clayton Christensen
author.heading: About Clayton Christensen
author.metaLine: 1952–2020 · Harvard Business School professor & theorist of disruptive innovation
author.bio: Clayton Magleby Christensen (born Salt Lake City, 6 April 1952; died Boston, 23 January 2020) was the Kim B. Clark Professor of Business Administration at Harvard Business School. He coined disruptive innovation in a 1995 article and developed it in The Innovator’s Dilemma (1997), which The Economist cited in calling him the most influential management thinker of his time. He wrote as readily about how to live as about how firms fail, and the two quotations here come from that second strand.

misattribution.heading: The half that goes missing
misattribution.intro: The attribution is not in dispute. What travels badly is the length.

items.who: “…as many ways to help others learn and grow.”
items.why: A full stop gets added where the original has a comma, which turns two-fifths of a sentence into a whole one. Christensen’s list does not stop there: it goes on to taking responsibility and being recognised for achievement, and to contributing to the success of a team.

misattribution.truthLine: The documented sentence ↗ runs to the end of that list — and the items it loses are the ones about being seen.

context.heading: Why he meant it literally
lead: Coming from the man who spent his career explaining how well-run companies fail, this reads oddly at first — management as the noble profession, not the necessary one. The sentence earns it by what follows the comma: the claim is not that managing is important, but that it is unusually well supplied with chances to do something for another person.
Read whole, it is an argument about opportunity rather than status. Read short, it is a compliment. The difference is the clauses that usually get cut.
context.pull: Not that the work matters. That the work keeps handing you chances to matter to someone.
